source.title: Some open questions in TDDFT: Clues from Lattice Models and Kadanoff-Baym Dynamics

accepted.question_text: How can time-dependent density-functional theory improve on the adiabatic local density approximation for lattice or continuum many-body systems by incorporating the full history dependence of the one-particle density, spatial nonlocality, and the ultranonlocal coupling between memory effects and spatial nonlocal effects in the exchange-correlation potential vxc? In this setting, TDDFT uses the one-particle density n as its central variable, vxc contains the many-body dynamical correlations, and ALDA replaces that history-dependent and spatially nonlocal object with a potential that depends only on the local density at the current time.

evidence.quote: In TDDFT, the key variable is the one-particle density n, and a central ingredient is the time-dependent exchange-correlation (XC) potential vxc, which incorporates all the complexities of the time-dependent many-body dynamics. As a result of this contracted description, and since time enters explicitly into the formulation, vxc depends in a highly non-trivial way on the entire history of the density n (memory effects).

An easy but inadequate way to proceed is to make use of the so-called adiabatic local density approximation (ALDA), where the XC potential at every particular time only depends on the local density. This amounts to neglecting non-locality in space and memory effects in vxc. In general, in order to improve the ALDA, it becomes necessary to consider the issue of ultranonlocality. This means that the introduction of non-locality in time requires the inclusion of strong non-local effects in space.

When non-local and non-adiabatic effects play an important role, i.e. for fast perturbations, the ALDA is clearly insufficient. This is especially evident if one compares the exact, TDDFT-ALDA and Kadanoff-Baym dynamics. In the latter, effects beyond the ALDA are present, and are seen to be necessary to get a good agreement with the exact data.

accepted.question_text: Can a practical exchange-correlation kernel fxc for linear-response TDDFT be constructed that is nonlocal and frequency dependent, improves systematically on ALDA, and avoids the unphysical poles caused by the linearized Sham-Schlueter or Klein-functional route, where double inversion of the non-interacting Kohn-Sham response function chi0 turns zeros of chi0 into double poles in fxc? One proposed direction is to start from the Luttinger-Ward functional rather than the Klein functional, but it remains open whether that avoids the known pathology without creating new ones.

evidence.quote: The drawback, however, is the lack of a systematic approach to finding successively better approximations to the exchange-correlation kernel which contains all the important particle-hole interactions beyond the random phase approximation (RPA).
Along these lines, a diagrammatic procedure for finding better kernels fxc:s was developed in Ref. [43], but it still remains untested.

From the defining equation above for the kernel fxc we see that one has to invert the response function chi0 twice in order to obtain fxc. Thus, a zero in chi0 produces a double pole in fxc which, in turn, causes the full response function chi to have an unphysical pole in the upper half plane.

There have been attempts to go beyond the ALDA and simultaneously include non-locality and frequency dependence in the kernel fxc. Several of these attempts have originated in the LSS or, equivalently, in the variational approach starting from the Klein functional, and have, therefore, led to severe difficulties as discussed in the introduction. The problem is associated with use of the LSS or, within the variational appoach, with starting from the Klein functional. The "perpetrator" is the double inversion of the chi0 within these formulations. We can already anticipate that this particular problem will not be present if one instead choses to start from the more sophisticated Luttinger and Ward (LW) functional [125]. Whether or not the LW functional will give rise to other problems remains to be seen. Work along these lines is underway.

accepted.question_text: Can density-based TDDFT on a lattice be given a fully rigorous Runge-Gross-type foundation, or otherwise characterized well enough to know when the density-potential mapping is unique and when heuristic use of lattice TDDFT is reliable? The problem is specific to lattice Hamiltonians because the usual reductio-ad-absurdum proof fails, examples contradict uniqueness of the correspondence between densities and potentials, and known v0-representability conditions are complete only in limited cases such as one particle on a one-dimensional lattice or special Hubbard dimers.
accepted.context_brief: Rigorous density mapping for lattice TDDFT

evidence.quote: As shown in [80], for a 1D lattice with L sites, the condition |Sk| <= 2 sqrt(nk nk+1), with Sk = sum from i=1 to k dot ni (this expresses current conservation), is necessary and sufficient for v0-representability for N = 1 particle.

The above condition for Sk is only a necessary one for N > 1 [39], also when Hubbard interactions are taken into account. For the special case of a dimer, and using the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, one can show that the exact density of a Hubbard dimer is v0-representable [39].

There is at present no formulation of the Runge-Gross (RG) theorem of TDDFT for the lattice. The reason for this has been explicitly discussed in [17] and, in essence, it has to do with the fact that a reductio ad absurdum strategy, along the lines of the RG theorem, is not possible.
This observation corroborates the fact that, for lattice Hamiltonians, one can actually find examples which contradict the uniqueness of the correspondence between densities and potentials.
It should, however, still be possible to use lattice TDDFT on heuristic grounds, even if, at present, the practical implications of the lack of a rigorous formulation largely remain to be seen.

accepted.question_text: What are the physical regimes and corrective principles for Kadanoff-Baym dynamics combined with many-body perturbation theory when conserving approximations still show fundamental failures, such as breakdown at strong interaction, artificial correlation-induced damping, questionable steady states in extended systems, and violations of positivity in two-particle correlation functions? The setting is the nonequilibrium Green's-function approach, where the Kadanoff-Baym equations use a self-energy from approximations such as second Born, GW, or T-matrix, which conserve macroscopic quantities but do not guarantee all physically required properties.

evidence.quote: All these approximations are conserving [40], i.e. the macroscopic conservation laws (for the energy, the number of particles, etc.) hold, which is a key requirement for time dynamics. The fact that the approximations are conserving does, however, not guarantee the soundness of other important features, as shown in the next Section.

On the more fundamental side, the NEG approach within MBPT manifests other undesirable traits, for example perturbation schemes may break down for strong interactions. However, even for converging schemes, unphysical features can emerge, which can sometimes play an important role.

Moreover, in the KBE-based time dynamics, the MBA:s introduce an artificial correlation induced damping which, in some cases, can completely dominate the evolution. For finite systems, such damped dynamics results in a steady (i.e. never decaying) state. In extended systems, a similar behavior is observed, but with a difference, namely arbitrarily long-lived states occur which, however, eventually decay into a unique steady state. This behavior is certainly artificial in finite systems, while its physical soundness in extended systems is much harder to establish.
However, within conserving MBA:s, correlation functions may violate important properties such as positiveness [117].

accepted.question_text: How can TDDFT linear-response approximations for the Hubbard lattice be improved so that short-range correlations are treated correctly and the local double occupancy dR = <nR up nR down>, computed from the density response function, remains physically positive? In the paper's 3D homogeneous Hubbard model tests, both RPA and ALDA can produce negative double occupancies even though double occupancy is manifestly positive, showing that ALDA inherits a short-range correlation failure known from continuum electron-gas response calculations.
accepted.context_brief: Positive double occupancy in response approximations

evidence.quote: In general, the pair correlation function (and thus the density response function) is a careful indicator of the accuracy of a many-body approximation. Thus, looking at properties which involve chi can provide a severe test to assess the performance of the ALDA.
The first is that in some cases the RPA and ALDA results for dR are negative. Since dR is manifestly positive, this is an adverse outcome of the ALDA, and is rather general in character.

As a conclusive remark, while our results for the double occupancy point out a shortcoming of the ALDA, they also indicate that the problem with the sign of dR could be less acute than in the continuum case. In fact, at least for the cases we considered, double occupancies in the ALDA are only slightly negative and, most likely, this is a consequence of the natural cut-off introduced by the lattice at short distances.

Furthermore, an ALDA treatment for the linear response of the 3D homogenous Hubbard model exhibits an important pitfall which is also present in the continuum case, namely short-range correlations are incorrectly accounted for by the ALDA, albeit at a lesser extent than for the electron gas.

accepted.question_text: How should exchange-correlation kernels for Hubbard lattice TDDFT account for qualitative features of the ALDA kernel that have no known continuum analogue, including a sign that changes with density and interaction strength, and a singularity at half filling for sufficiently large interaction U caused by the discontinuity of vxc at the Mott-Hubbard metal-insulator transition? The paper expects these features to persist when nonlocal and nonadiabatic effects are added, so a complete theory must explain how they affect density response beyond the local adiabatic limit.

evidence.quote: In Fig. 3, we see clearly one of the interesting features of fALDA xc, namely the XC kernel can be either negative or positive [119]. This is especially evident for U = 8, and can also immediately be gathered from the results for vxc in Fig. 1. Thus we see that, depending on the band filling, fALDA xc can reduce or reinforce the effect of the bare interaction U in Eq. (31).

Looking again at Fig. 1, we note that the discontinuity in vDMFT xc for U > U Mott c (in our case U = 24) will introduce a (Dirac's delta-like) spike in the XC kernel at n = 1. This singular behavior would be absent for U < U Mott c in 3D, but always present in 1D where vxc is discontinuous for any value of U.

We have also shown that the sign of the ALDA XC kernel can change depending on the values of U and the density, and that for large enough values of U, fxc can exhibit a singular behavior at half-filling (due to the discontinuity in vxc, which in turn is indicative of the Mott-Hubbard metal-insulator transition). Such characteristics of fxc are clearly visible in the energy dependence of the density response function. To our knowledge, the qualitative features of fALDA xc just mentioned have no correspondence in the available XC kernels for continuum case. On general grounds, we expect they should be robust against the inclusion of non-local, non-adiabatic effects.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Can Quantum Monte Carlo or Gutzwiller approximation calculations provide alternative exchange-correlation energies for the homogeneous 3D Hubbard model?

evidence.quote: It is perhaps worth mentioning that schemes other than DMFT could be used to determine the exc of the homogenous system, e.g. the Quantum Monte Carlo method or the Gutzwiller approximation (such work is currently under way).

Extracted the ALDA improvement issue from the discussion of memory, spatial nonlocality, and ultranonlocality.
Extracted the kernel-construction issue from the linear response section and conclusions, including untested diagrammatic kernels, chi0 double inversion, and the Luttinger-Ward direction.
Extracted the lattice density-mapping issue from v0-representability limits, lack of a lattice Runge-Gross theorem, and unresolved practical implications.
Extracted KBE plus MBPT limitations from the drawbacks subsection, including strong-interaction breakdown, artificial damping, steady-state concerns, and positivity violations.
Extracted ALDA response issues involving negative double occupancy and the qualitative behavior of sign-changing or singular Hubbard kernels.
Expanded ALDA improvement into a self-contained question using the paper's definition of TDDFT variables, vxc history dependence, ALDA, and ultranonlocality.
Merged the untested diagrammatic-kernel issue with the LSS and Klein-functional pathology because both concern constructing practical nonlocal frequency-dependent fxc kernels beyond ALDA.
Expanded lattice Runge-Gross and v0-representability statements into a self-contained question about density-potential mapping and practical reliability.
Expanded KBE plus MBPT drawbacks into a self-contained question about regimes and corrective principles while preserving the stated scope of conserving approximations.
Expanded negative double occupancy into a self-contained question about correcting short-range correlations in TDDFT response approximations.
Expanded the sign-changing and singular ALDA kernel discussion into a self-contained question about Hubbard-kernel features beyond the local adiabatic limit.
